update.title: RISC-V: Support vector initialization from two halves
update.body:
This patch adds vec_concat and vec_init expanders to construct a full
vector from two half-width vectors (e.g. [0 1 2 3] + [4 5 6 7] ->
[0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7]) via vslideup.

Key changes:
- Implement @vec_concat and vec_init expanders, restricted to LMUL <= 1.
- Extend VLS_HAS_HALF to include Float16 (HF) and BFloat16 (BF) modes.
- Add VLA_HAS_HALF to support VLA modes.
- Unify them under V_HAS_HALF and generalize V_HALF/v_half (also updating
  vec_extract).
- Update comments in shuffle_even_odd_patterns.

Changes in v2:
- Restrict vec_concat and vec_init to LMUL <= 1 to avoid multi-register spills.
- Revert changes in shuffle_even_odd_patterns: vec_concat doesn't handle
  mixed modes, using vec_concat while keeping a fallback makes the code messy,
  so just update comments.
- Update vec-concat-1.c slideup expectations and comments.

Regtested on rv64gcv.

gcc/ChangeLog:

	* config/riscv/autovec.md (vec_init<mode><v_half>): New expander.
	(vec_extract<mode><v_half>): Use <V_HALF>.
	* config/riscv/riscv-v.cc (shuffle_even_odd_patterns): Update
	comments.
	* config/riscv/vector.md (@vec_concat<mode>): New expander.
	* config/riscv/vector-iterators.md (VLS_HAS_HALF): Add HF and BF modes.
	(VLA_HAS_HALF, V_HAS_HALF): New mode iterators.
	(V_HALF, v_half): Rename from VLS_HALF and vls_half.

update.title: sched: Avoid creating fusion groups during selective scheduling
update.body:
Selective scheduling builds its instruction expressions after the
initial Haifa dependency analysis.  Reanalyzing instructions later can
set SCHED_GROUP_P without updating VINSN_UNIQUE_P or the group links.
This can make sel_rank_for_schedule violate comparator antisymmetry
and trigger an ICE with checking enabled.

Only create macro-fusion groups during Haifa dependency analysis,
including the initial Haifa emulation used by selective scheduling.
Add RTL regressions using the existing XiangShan zero-extension
fusion rules.  Check that initial grouping still runs and that
scheduling does not create a new group for initially separated shifts.
A loop variant reproduces the comparator ICE during software pipelining.

The regression tests were generated with LLM assistance.

gcc/ChangeLog:

	* sched-deps.cc (sched_analyze_insn): Restrict macro-fusion grouping
	to Haifa dependency analysis.

gcc/testsuite/ChangeLog:

	* gcc.target/riscv/sched-fusion-selective.c: New test.
	* gcc.target/riscv/sched-fusion-selective-ice.c: Likewise.

Signed-off-by: Jin Ma <jinma@linux.alibaba.com>

update.title: [RISC-V][PR 127813] Add more czero patterns/splitters for RISC-V
update.body:
So the first new pattern here is very straightforward.  It's essentially the
same pattern the VRULL guys did initially and I suggested they move towards the
if-then-else form.  This bug clearly shows that pattern useful.

The two other patterns are more interesting.

We'd really like to match the (and (neg (reg1)) (reg2)) when reg1 has a 0/1
value as a czero, similarly for the inverse which uses (plus (reg1) (const_int
-1)).   My first implementation checked nonzero_bits and matched that form
directly generating the czero.  Review via an LLM flagged that problem.

For this testcase (and I think reasonably generally) we'll often see these
wrapped by an IOR as part of a more general conditional move sequence
constructed from logicals with the IOR doing final selection.  So that's a 3->2
split that we can recognize in combine (using nonzero_bits), then immediately
rewrite into a form that doesn't require that test.  It's not ideal, but should
be enough to capture the most common cases.

Tested on riscv32-elf and riscv64-elf and bootstrapped and regression tested on
the k3.  c920 is being flaky so that'll have to spin overnight.  k1 is queued
and will pick this up on its next run which starts in an hour or two.

Anyway, pushing this to the trunk.  I'll keep the BZ open as Andrea wants to
tackle some stuff up in match.pd in a generic way.

	PR tree-optimization/127813
gcc/
	* config/riscv/zicond.md: Add new define_insn for czero expressed via
	logical ops.  Add define_splits when related patterns are used by an
	IOR to select across two values.

gcc/testsuite
	* gcc.target/riscv/pr127813.c: New test.

update.title: [RISC-V] Fix mode goofs in RISC-V's bitmanip.md
update.body:
So two more issues in bitmanip.md found by LLM review.

We should never have mismatched modes between the mode of an operator such as
AND and the modes of its operands.  Two patterns still have that bug in
bitmanip.md.

In this case the patters are conditional on TARGET_64BIT, so X is always DI.
Additionally, the SI operation really should just have been DI.  My first
thought was to remove the patterns as they shouldn't have been matching, but
that regresses in the testsuite.  My guess is in the IL we've got a subreg
sitting in there and the pattern matched the narrowing subreg as the SI
argument.  We can just take the full DI value instead and the right things just
happen (we're masking off all but a few of the low bits as these are
shift/rotate counts).

Tested on riscv32-elf and riscv64-elf and bootstrap + regression tested on k3
and c920.  Pushing to the trunk.  LLM is still finding things of interest in
here...

gcc/
	* config/riscv/bitmanip.md (*<bitmanip_optab>3_mask_si): Fix mode
	for masked shift count.
	(*<bitmanip_optab>si3_sext_mask): Likewise.

update.title: [RISC-V] Fix LLM identified bugs in RISC-V bitmanip.md file
update.body:
So as I mentioned at Cauldron I think we can and should be proactively looking
at our machine descriptions with LLMs for bugs. This patch addresses four
issues caught by an LLM checker on RISC-V's bitmanip.md.

First we have a a simply broken pattern.  The pattern incorrectly uses sext_hwi
(operand, 32) > 0 to see if it's safe to treat a constant as if it's been
extended from 32 to 64 bits.  But it'll fails miserably if the constant has any
bits in 32..63 already set, it essentially wipes them out when they may be
relevant to the min/max comparison.  I spent an absurd amount of time trying to
get a C testcase that would trigger.  I did finally get one to trigger using
RTL, but it triggers an ICE later when mated with a driver to send
problematical constants into the key function.

Given the pattern has been problematical before, the original introduction said
it was supposed to be a short-term fix and my inability to trigger with C code,
I'm just going to remove the pattern.

Next we have a clobber operand in "X" mode in a splitter.  The other operands
are GPR.  In the split-rtl we use that as as scratch and can end up with
mismatched modes.  Changing it to GPR is the right thing to do.

Next we have a pattern that I'm sure shouldn't match anything.  It's condition
is TARGET_64BIT so the mode of its AND operation is DI.  Yet the AND has two SI
operands.  Opps.  This one looks familiar to me, so probably something I
introduced.

Last, there's a pattern which generates RTL designed to match a Zbs bit
extraction, but the splitter was not conditional on Zbs.  This isn't generally
causing problems because combine will ignore the splitter if it generates RTL
that doesn't match.  But we might as well do the right thing and add the
TARGET_ZBS condition.

Regression tested on riscv32-elf and riscv64-elf.  Pushing to the trunk.

Assisted-by: LLM (reviewing bitmanip.md for bugs, attempts to generate testcase
for first problem)

Jeff

ps.  There are other problems in this file, but these were easy to knock out.

	* config/riscv/bitmanip.md (minmax splitter): Remove broken pattern.
	(*bextdi_position_ze_masked): Likewise.
	(polarity reversed mask splitter): Clobber GPR, not X mode register.
	(splitter to generate bext): Make conditional on TARGET_ZBS.

update.title: [PATCH] rtl, aarch64, riscv: Ignore leading debug insns [PR127934, PR127936]
update.body:
Both rest_of_insert_bti and riscv_mode_needed need the first executable
instruction in the function, but get_first_nonnote_insn can return a leading
DEBUG_INSN.  This makes their decisions depend on debug information.

On AArch64 this can add a redundant BTI C before PACIASP.  On RISC-V it can
prevent a singleton VXRM setting from being hoisted to the function entry.

Add get_first_nonnote_nondebug_insn and use it at both sites.  Add regression
tests that check both -fcompare-debug and the expected generated code.

Tested at b3a3ecc46023 on x86_64-pc-linux-gnu with a native bootstrap and
the gcc and g++ testsuites, comparing unmodified and patched trees.  The
summary counts and sorted FAIL lines are unchanged.  The focused AArch64 and
RISC-V tests also pass with the patch and fail without it.

	PR target/127936

update.title: riscv: Avoid R_RISCV_JAL for __sigjmp_save
update.body:
The `j` pseudo-instruction uses an R_RISCV_JAL relocation, limiting the
target to the JAL ±1 MiB range. PGO/LTO function/section reordering
may place `__sigjmp_save` outside this range and cause the final link
to fail.

Use `tail` instead, which emits R_RISCV_CALL_PLT and permits the linker
to relax the call when possible.

Signed-off-by: Mingliang Liu <liumingliang.dev@bytedance.com>
Reviewed-by: Peter Bergner <bergner@tenstorrent.com>

update.title: RISC-V: Model ALU insn scheduling as ALU0 or ALU1 for SpacemiT-X60

Based on micro-architectural testing of Spacemit-X60 ALU instructions
they reserve only one of the two ALU units available on the CPU.
Modeling the reservation of ALU instructions as ALU0 or ALU1 moves the
needle slightly.

Benchmark of coremark executed with perf:
 taskset -c 0 perf stat -r 10 -e cycles,instructions ./coremark.exe

-mtune=spacemit-x60 -march=rv64gc_zba_zbb_zbs -O2
                    current                                            new
  cycles    29,442,732,143 +-0.11%        28,892,288,831 +-0.07%
  insns      31,451,155,580 +-0.03%        31,450,458,048 +-0.03%
  IPC          1.07                                                   1.09
  time (s)  18.4061 +-0.0209                       18.0631 +-0.0131

-mcpu=spacemit-x60 -O2
                    current                                            new
  cycles     29,715,461,331 +-0.11%       29,622,701,777 +-0.10%
  insns       29,679,069,220 +-0.03%       29,678,356,566 +-0.03%
  IPC           1.00                                                 1.00
  time (s)   18.5767 +-0.0203                     18.5192 +-0.0191

-mcpu=spacemit-x60 -O2 -funroll-loops
                       current                                            new
  cycles       28,212,445,245 +-0.12%        27,933,417,579 +-0.07%

update.title: [RISC-V][PR target/127778] Use synthesize_add more on RISC-V
update.body:
As the pr127778 shows the changes to generally improve how we synthesize x+C
regressed a class of cases, particularly those with C in the range [2048..4095]
that are used as an address for a memory reference during initial RTL
generation.

The problem can be seen in this .expand fragment:

(insn 7 4 8 2 (set (reg:DI 136)
        (const_int 4096 [0x1000])) "j.c":4:11 -1
     (nil))
(insn 8 7 9 2 (set (reg/f:DI 137)
        (plus:DI (reg/v/f:DI 134 [ p ])
            (reg:DI 136))) "j.c":4:11 -1
     (nil))
(insn 9 8 0 2 (set (mem:SI (plus:DI (reg/f:DI 137)
                (const_int -96 [0xffffffffffffffa0])) [1 MEM[(int *)p_1(D) + 4000B]+0 S4 A32])
        (subreg/s/u:SI (reg/v:DI 135 [ v ]) 0)) "j.c":4:11 -1
     (nil))

So we're not using add synthesis, but instead falling back to naive code
generation.  It turns out there's a path through the RISC-V target files which
avoids the add expanders.  So while we could try to recover good code
generation later, it seems much better to just generate reasonable code at the
gimple-RTL phase.

This patch intercepts the path through riscv_add_offset and will use
synthesize_add when possible.  So we get this kind of initial RTL instead:

(insn 7 4 8 2 (set (reg/f:SI 136)
        (plus:SI (reg/v/f:SI 134 [ p ])
            (const_int 1953 [0x7a1]))) "j.c":4:15 -1
     (nil))
(insn 8 7 9 2 (set (reg/f:SI 136)
        (plus:SI (reg/f:SI 136)
            (const_int 2047 [0x7ff]))) "j.c":4:15 -1
     (nil))
(insn 9 8 0 2 (set (mem:SI (reg/f:SI 136) [1 MEM[(int *)p_1(D) + 4000B]+0 S4 A32])
        (reg/v:SI 135 [ v ])) "j.c":4:15 -1
     (nil))

It's trivial to combine insn 8 and insn 9 resulting in the final code
generation we want to see.

We still bypass the synthesis code when presented with the code in pr105733:

> #define BUF_SIZE 2064
>
> void
> foo(unsigned long i)
> {
>    volatile char buf[BUF_SIZE];
>
>    buf[i] = 0;
> }
>
In this case the offset is going to be formed with virtual-stack-vars. That
later gets turned into sp+offset.  Anyway, the initial code generation for that
case looks like this if we're not careful:

(insn 6 3 7 2 (set (reg/f:SI 135)
       (plus:SI (reg/f:SI 129 virtual-stack-vars)
           (const_int -16 [0xfffffffffffffff0]))) "j.c":8:12 -1
    (nil))
(insn 7 6 8 2 (set (reg/f:SI 135)
       (plus:SI (reg/f:SI 135)
           (const_int -2048 [0xfffffffffffff800]))) "j.c":8:12 -1
    (nil))
(insn 8 7 9 2 (set (reg/f:SI 136)
       (plus:SI (reg/f:SI 135)
           (reg/v:SI 134 [ i ]))) "j.c":8:12 -1
    (nil))
(insn 9 8 0 2 (set (mem/v:QI (reg/f:SI 136) [0 buf[i_2(D)]+0 S1 A8])
       (const_int 0 [0])) "j.c":8:12 -1
    (nil))

In this case we'd be dependent upon something rewriting this mess to push the
constant offset down into the mem, and clean up the virtual-stack-vars
reference post-reload.  fold-mem-offsets would be the natural choice.  But it's
easy enough to special case the base registers that get eliminated so that the
initial RTL we generate looks like this:

(insn 6 3 7 2 (set (reg:SI 135)
        (const_int -4096 [0xfffffffffffff000])) "j.c":8:12 -1
     (nil))
(insn 7 6 8 2 (set (reg/f:SI 136)
        (plus:SI (reg/f:SI 129 virtual-stack-vars)
            (reg:SI 135))) "j.c":8:12 -1
     (nil))
(insn 8 7 9 2 (set (reg/f:SI 137)
        (plus:SI (reg/f:SI 136)
            (reg/v:SI 134 [ i ]))) "j.c":8:12 -1
     (nil))
(insn 9 8 0 2 (set (mem/v:QI (plus:SI (reg/f:SI 137)
                (const_int 2032 [0x7f0])) [0 buf[i_2(D)]+0 S1 A8])
        (const_int 0 [0])) "j.c":8:12 -1
     (nil))

Which avoids regressing pr105733.  There's still some cruft in the final
assembly, but I think that's ultimately a failing of fold-mem-offsets that I
haven't chased down.  I'll get that cruft filed as a distinct bug against
f-m-o.

Tested on riscv32-elf and riscv64-elf.  I don't recall if this made it into my
tester's git repo early enough to make the overnight bootstraps.  Regardless,

update.title: lower-subreg: Don't decompose pre-existing concatns. [PR127443]
update.body:
Lower-subreg decomposes concatn subregs.  Since the regmode-natural-size
changes we could trigger an ICE by insisting the inner mode is
splittable into words.  But the CONCATN handling in lower-subreg is
specifically for the CONCATNs that lower-subreg.cc itself creates, rather
than a general operation.  For example, other parts of the file assume
that a CONCATN has exactly two operands.  There are also other asserts
that could trigger for preexisting CONCATNs.

This patch sets a flag on these temporary CONCATNs to distinguish them from
preexisting CONCATNs.  'volatil' is free and is used in a similar
fashion by var-tracking.cc (for CONCAT rather than CONCATN).

Co-Authored-By: Richard Sandiford <rdsandiford@googlemail.com>

	PR rtl-optimization/127443

gcc/ChangeLog:

	* lower-subreg.cc (DECOMPOSED_REGISTER_P): New macro.
	(decompose_register): Mark decomposed.
	(resolve_reg_p): Only resolve decomposed regs.
	(resolve_subreg_p): Move.
	(simplify_subreg_concatn): Remove assert.
	(simplify_gen_subreg_concatn): Use resolve_subreg_p.
	(resolve_operand_for_swap_move_operator): Adjust assert.
	(resolve_debug): Unmark as decomposed.
	* rtl.h (struct GTY): Document usage of volatil in lower-subreg.
